newsitem.title: USA: Detroit Edison files stranded cost adjustment plan.
newsitem.headline: Detroit Edison files stranded cost adjustment plan.

text.p: DTE Energy Co's Detroit Edison Co on Wednesday sent the Michigan Public Service Commission (MPSC) a proposal on how its rates should be adjusted so it can recover its stranded costs.

MSCP asked Michigan's two investor-owned utilities, Detroit Edison and Consumers Energy Co, a subsidiary of CMS Energy Co, to propose a "true-up" mechanism as part of its studies into restructuring the state's power industry.
As the entire power industry moves toward a deregulated market, "true-up" plans are seen as way utilities can protect themselves if transition charges fail to cover their stranded costs.
Stranded costs are investments, mostly in power plants, that are uneconomic in a competitive environment, where they can no longer be passed down to the consumer.
Detroit Edison estimates its stranded costs at $5.4 billion.
Transition charges, designed to cover these costs, are imposed on customers who elect to drop their traditional local utility and buy their electricity from some other supplier.

Detroit Edison, in a summary of the proposal, said its adjustment plan is based on actual market clearing prices (MCP) that will be reviewed annually. Any variations between the projected and actual MCP would be added or subtracted to the transition charges to be collected the following year.
The company proposes the initial transition charge be set at 0.43 cents per kilowatt-hour (KWh).

In the beginning, the actual MCP would be established by using the Michigan Electric Coordinated System (MECS) average system "lambda" for energy plus 0.5 cents/KWh for generation capacity, Detroit Edison said.
MECS' system lambda is defined as the highest cost hourly power in use by the system.
Eventually, the actual MCP would be determined by a market index or a basket of indices, which would be compared with Detroit Edison's projected MCP.

In the "true-up" plan submitted Monday by Consumers Energy, Consumers proposed its MCP be based on the results of its planned auction of 600 megawatts of power supply contracts over the next four years.
The sale of this capacity will establish a benchmark against which to measure its stranded costs, Consumers said.
